newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Guatemala and China talk on U.N. peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala and China talk on U.N. peacekeepers.

text.p: Guatemala and China on Wednesday held secret talks in an effort to repair the effects of Beijing's veto that barred U.N. observers from monitoring a peace pact in the Central American country, diplomats said.
The envoys said China was showing some flexibility on the issue but they did not expect immediate results to undo Beijing's negative vote in the Security Council last Friday.
The 14 other council members all supported sending 155 military observers to Guatemala for three months to monitor the U.N.-brokered peace agreements that ended more than three decades of civil war.
"Our door is always open," said Chen Ranfeng, China's U.N. spokesman in reference to discussions with Guatemala.

China has objected to Guatemala's ties to Taiwan, its support of moves to get U.N. membership for Taipei and its invitation to Taiwan's foreign minister John Chang to attend the peace accord signing ceremonies on Dec. 29.

The veto was China's first in nearly 25 years and has unleashed harsh criticism, particularly among Latin American nations. China regards Taiwan as a renegade province that will one day be reunited with the motherland.
Diplomats said there were three alternatives to fulfil the Guatemalan peace accords. They were:
-- to resubmit the issue to the Security Council should China and Guatemala reach any understanding.

-- to go to the General Assembly, which originally approved the 500-strong U.N. human rights monitoring mission in Guatemala and already has a few military observers. But the United States was said to be anxious not to set a precedent by having the Third World dominated assembly override Security Council actions. And China, which considers itself a champion of the developing world, did not want to embarrassed by losing a vote in the assembly, the diplomats said.

-- to ask the Organisation of American States to field the observers under its auspices. But envoys said the OAS was reluctant to undertake anything related to military activities, sensitive to past U.S. armed action in the region. They also said all factions in Guatemala preferred the United Nations as the accords stated.

The issue has been discussed almost daily among the so-called "friends of Guatemala" who have been helping the United Nations in the peace process. They are the United States, Mexico, Spain, Colombia, Norway and Venezuela.
China raised similar objections last year when it balked at renewing a later U.N. peacekeeping force in Haiti.

After holding the Haiti operation hostage for several days, China finally relented and voted for a scaled-down compromise and a Chinese diplomatic delegation visited Haiti last July for the first time in 40 years.

One senior Western diplomat said he suspected China became emboldened on the Taiwan issue in the United Nations since the last Haiti resolution, mainly because South Africa had broken diplomatic ties to Taiwan and recognised Beijing.
